metaDesc: The top 10 most popular restaurants in Tak Province 2026 — from Chidchol on the Ping River to B. Kung Pao Mae Sot, the legendary clay-pot roti, Tuay Khao Soi, and Baan Pak Rak Tawan. Includes signature dishes, prices, and planning tips.

ogTitle: 10 Most Popular Restaurants in Tak Province 2026
ogDesc: Eat your way through Tak like a local — from Tak city on the Ping River to border-town bites in Mae Sot: seafood, khao soi, clay-pot roti, and Tak-style noodles, all in one list.
eyebrow: Eat Like a Tak Local · Updated 2026
intro: Tak is a province where great food hides across two very different zones. On the Tak city side, along the Ping River, you'll find riverside Thai restaurants and a style of noodles unique to this town. Cross over to Mae Sot near the Myanmar border and you enter another world — fresh seafood, khao soi, clay-baked roti, and dim sum you won't easily find elsewhere. We've pulled together 10 restaurants that locals actually eat at and that travelers mention most.
chips: 🌊 Thai Riverside Dining on the Ping

blocks.html:
The charm of eating in Tak is that a single province offers so many different flavors. Start the morning on the Tak city side with a bowl of thin-noodle Tak-style noodles topped with dried shrimp powder and pork crackling, right by the Ping River. Mid-morning, drive north and stop at a café tucked in a rice-paddy landscape at Mai Ngam. By evening, cross to Mae Sot — a town that feels like a different country — full of markets and food that blends Shan, Burmese, and Thai. There are fat grilled river prawns, fragrant chicken khao soi, and clay-pot roti baked in an earthen oven that sells out well before 8 a.m. This is a province where one trip covers local home-style food, riverside dining, and border-town street eats.

Several restaurants on this list are genuine local institutions. The legendary clay-pot roti in Mae Sot has been open for over half a century and is credited as the first of its kind in Thailand. Tuay Khao Soi has been serving since 1969 — locals rate its halal chicken khao soi as the best in the district. B. Kung Pao Mae Sot has been grilling river prawns for more than twenty years and is the go-to destination for seafood lovers. On the Tak city side, Chidchol and Aiyarawadee offer Thai food with Ping River views, while Baan Pak Rak Tawan near Mae To is a road-trip stop, an organic-vegetable restaurant, and the place to try miang jom pol — one of Tak's signature bites. If you're passing through, pull over and taste a couple of these. You'll understand why people keep talking about them.

blocks.name: Chidchol
blocks.signature: Chidchol Chicken, Chidchol Stir-fried Glass Noodles, Tak-style Nam Phrik Dam Set, Tom Yam Catfish
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Tak city and want a meal you'll remember, Chidchol is one of the first names locals bring up. This venerable restaurant has been open for nearly fifty years, sitting on the banks of the Ping River in a beautiful traditional Thai wooden house surrounded by a shady garden. Tables along the riverbank look out over the bridge crossing — a perfect setting for a first meal in the province, a family lunch, or a relaxed dinner with older relatives.

The dish everyone orders is Chidchol Chicken — the house signature. The chicken is steamed through, then deep-fried whole until the skin turns crisp while the flesh stays juicy. It arrives over crispy egg noodles with the restaurant's house sauce. Reviewers consistently say the meat is more tender than expected and pairs with the crunchy noodles in a surprisingly good way. Another popular order is the Chidchol stir-fried glass noodles, rounded and well-seasoned. For those who want bold Northern Thai flavors, the Tak-style nam phrik dam set — eaten with fresh vegetables and accompaniments — is the one to try. The tom yam catfish delivers firm flesh and an intensely rich broth.

Many reviews describe a homespun, old-school quality — like a meal from a relative's kitchen. The owner is praised for being warm and attentive. The restaurant carries Wongnai Users' Choice awards for 2020 and 2021 and holds around 4.0 stars from over a hundred Wongnai reviews. Prices run 80–400 THB per dish — great value for a meal that delivers both flavor and atmosphere.

The restaurant is a short distance from the city centre, set riverside with clear signage and parking. Hours are approximately 10:00–21:00 most days. On weekends it fills up — call ahead if you're coming in a group or want a riverside table.
blocks.bestFor: First meal in the province; relaxed family dining by the river
blocks.spice: Medium — spicy if you order nam phrik/tom yam

blocks.name: Thiengna Coffee and Bakery Farm
blocks.area: Phahon Yothin Rd, Mai Ngam Sub-district, Mueang Tak District, Tak Province
blocks.signature: Crispy Pork Stir-fried with Garlic and Onsen Egg on Rice, Pan-fried Egg, Nutella Banana Croissant, Matcha Uji Iced Drink
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving north through Tak and looking for a stop, Thiengna Coffee and Bakery Farm is the name almost every local will give you. This is the original Thiengna — the one that launched a brand now known all the way to Bangkok — open for over ten years. The shop occupies a tall vintage wooden house surrounded by greenery, large trees, and a waterside seating area. It's ideal for travelers who want to rest with coffee, croissant hunters tracking fresh bakes, or families who want a quiet breakfast in a breezy, shaded setting.

The most talked-about item is the daily-baked croissant — layered, crisp outside, soft inside. The Nutella banana version strikes a perfect sweet-rich note. For morning visitors, the crispy pork stir-fried with garlic and onsen egg is a crowd favourite: crunchy pork meets a runny onsen egg, and the pan-fried egg alongside it makes a satisfying breakfast. On the drinks side, the matcha uji iced drink is deep and smooth for green-tea fans. Most reviews praise the baked goods and the coffee. A few mention prices are slightly high for portions, but repeat visitors keep coming back for the atmosphere and the fresh bakes.

Prices start around 60 THB for pastries, up to 95–170 THB for drinks and food plates — fair for a café of this quality. The shop sits on Phahon Yothin Road in Mai Ngam sub-district, northbound side, easy to spot with parking available. Open daily 08:00–18:00. Free Wi-Fi, credit cards accepted, pet-friendly.

On long weekends the popular croissants sell out fast. Come early if you want your first choice, or call ahead to reserve. Anyone passing through Tak really should stop at least once.
mustOrder: Crispy Pork Stir-fried with Garlic and Onsen Egg on Rice
blocks.bestFor: Breakfast or a mid-drive stop heading north; café and fresh bakery lovers
blocks.spice: Mild (the garlic-pork rice dish can be adjusted)

blocks.name: B. Kung Pao Mae Sot
blocks.signature: Grilled River Prawns, Fish-sauce Marinated Crab Roe, Fresh Oysters, Stir-fried Spicy Catfish
blocks.descHtml:
Ask anyone in Mae Sot where to go for seafood and B. Kung Pao (Hia Biew) is typically the first name out. This restaurant has been a fixture of Mae Sot for over twenty years and is credited as one of the town's original grilled-prawn spots. The appeal is fresh produce sourced directly from across the Myanmar border. It's a great choice for a family seafood feast or a big group dinner — no need to drive to the coast to get impressive river prawns.

The dish at every table is the grilled river prawn — large, fatty, firm and springy. Reviews consistently praise the sweetness of the flesh and the intense prawn butter that begs to be dipped in the house seafood sauce. Another essential is the fish-sauce marinated crab roe: salty-sweet and perfectly rounded with hot steamed rice. Those who like fresh bivalves should try the plump fresh oysters, and if you want something punchy, order the Myanmar catfish stir-fried hot and spicy with fingerroot and holy basil — a real appetite-opener. Other popular choices include water spinach in oyster sauce, grilled freshwater clams, and oyster omelette.

The dining room is comfortable, with both air-conditioned and outdoor sections, wide tables, and easy parking. It's built for long, leisurely meals. Prices are reasonable for the freshness on offer — dishes run 100–600 THB, and river prawns are priced by weight. For groups, expect to spend 500 THB or more per person. Ask the per-kilogram price before ordering so you can plan your budget comfortably.

The restaurant is easy to find on the Asia Highway, about 50 metres past Hop Inn hotel. Open daily 16:00–23:00. On holidays and festivals the place fills up fast — call ahead for a group reservation.
blocks.bestFor: Dinner of river prawns with family or friends
blocks.spice: Adjustable — stir-fried spicy / yam dishes are medium-hot

blocks.name: Legendary Clay-Pot Roti — First in Thailand
blocks.signature: Clay-oven Roti — crisp outside, soft inside; Lentil Curry, Hot Thai-Muslim Tea, Hot Goat's Milk
blocks.descHtml:
If you wake up in Mae Sot unsure where to eat, head to the Legendary Clay-Pot Roti — First in Thailand, a tiny shop on Si Phanit Road opposite the livestock office. This place has been baking roti inside a clay pot over charcoal for more than 50 years and is now inseparable from the town. Locals call it clay-pot roti because instead of frying in a wok of oil, the dough is slapped directly onto the hot interior wall of a clay urn fired from the inside with charcoal — the result is an oil-free roti. It's ideal for anyone who loves traditional food and wants to start the day with something light but filling.

Order the hot clay-pot roti with sweetened condensed milk for dipping. The large discs are crisp outside and soft inside — the dough is hand-kneaded from 1 a.m. to 4 a.m. every day, and hundreds of pieces are made daily. Reviewers consistently note the perfectly chewy texture and a gentle toasty aroma from the clay pot. Pair it with Burmese-style hot milk tea or a soft-boiled egg. Weekend visitors can also get lentil curry on the side. Goat's milk and fresh cow's milk are available too.

Prices are extremely friendly — roti runs about 10–30 THB per piece, drinks are in the low tens of baht, and a satisfying meal won't reach 100 THB. The atmosphere is an old-fashioned morning shop, and every morning it fills with both Mae Sot residents and visitors queuing for roti straight from the pot. Opens from 5 a.m. until around 9 a.m., but many days everything is gone by 8:00–8:30. Come early if you don't want to miss out. Seating is limited, and for the lentil curry you need to aim for a weekend.
mustOrder: Clay-pot Roti with Sweetened Condensed Milk
blocks.bestFor: An early breakfast — join the queue for hot roti before it sells out
blocks.spice: Not spicy (can be with lentil curry on weekends)

blocks.name: Kwaytiaw Baan Din Mae Sot
blocks.signature: Braised Beef Egg Noodles, Clear Fishball Rice Noodle Soup, Mixed Pork Noodles
blocks.descHtml:
Ask people in Mae Sot which noodle shop to try and Kwaytiaw Baan Din comes up almost every time. The shop is in the Mae Pa sub-district area and has been open since 2003. What makes it memorable is the setting — the walls are built from real earth clay, decorated with vintage objects and old motorbikes reflecting the owner's love of bikes. The atmosphere feels more like a stylish shack than a regular noodle shop. It's a great mid-day stop for a good, wallet-friendly bowl, or for anyone who wants a restaurant with real character and good photo angles.

The orders that come up most consistently in reviews are the braised beef egg noodles — the beef simmers until tender and soaks up the broth — followed by the clear fishball rice noodle soup, whose broth is rounded and naturally sweet from the bone stock, and the mixed pork noodle bowl, which comes generously loaded. Several regulars love ordering a large bowl with chunky chicken drumsticks; reviewers say it's filling enough to last until late afternoon. The broth here is known for its depth — not thin, not over-seasoned. Those who like offal can add a mixed-organ topping.

Prices start around 40 THB, a standard bowl around 60 THB, and a loaded special around 70 THB — easily a meal under 100 THB. The shop opens from roughly 7–8 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily. One advantage is staying open through the afternoon when many other places close. The location is in a lane in the Mae Pa area; parking is available but crowded around noon.

The lunch rush gets very busy — expect a short wait. The open-air layout stays warm and airy but can be hot on sunny middays. Staff often speak Burmese; pointing at the menu works fine. For a shorter wait, arrive before noon or late afternoon.
blocks.bestFor: Lunch — a good bowl on a budget
blocks.spice: Season to taste at the table

blocks.name: Tuay Khao Soi Mae Sot
blocks.signature: Halal Chicken Khao Soi, add egg / extra chicken / extra noodles
blocks.descHtml:
Ask anyone in Mae Sot which khao soi is best and more than half will say Tuay Khao Soi — a small shop on Prasat Withi Road in the old town area. It has been serving since 1969, when a bowl cost 50 satang. Over fifty years later it still starts at just over thirty baht. This is a Muslim khao soi shop: only chicken, no pork, no beef. That makes it the default for halal diners and for travelers looking for something honest with a long story. It's a perfect first meal when you arrive in Mae Sot.

The main event is the chicken khao soi. What sets it apart from others is the house-made noodle — bouncy strands topped with deep-fried crispy noodles. The curry broth is described as smooth and gentle, not cloying sweet, not aggressively spiced. Reviewers say it's fragrant and comforting — the kind you finish to the last drop. Add an egg, extra chicken, or extra noodles to build up the bowl. It comes with house-pickled vegetables fermented in coconut water and vinegar for about a week, giving a mild sourness that cuts through the richness perfectly.

The setting is a simple shophouse with an open kitchen where you can watch noodles being blanched and eggs cracked right in front of you. Reviews praise the cleanliness and the quality of the utensils. Prices start around 35 THB; with add-ons it's still well under 100 THB per person. Open in two shifts — morning to early afternoon and evening to late night. If you're coming at midday, allow some extra time as it can get busy. One note from reviewers: sometimes the broth could be hotter. Overall, it's the original khao soi institution of Mae Sot — worth the stop.
mustOrder: Chicken Khao Soi with Extra Egg
blocks.bestFor: First meal in Mae Sot; khao soi fans seeking the original
blocks.libCredit: Illustration: Khao Soi · Rushen / Wikimedia (CC BY-SA 2.0)

blocks.name: Kwaytiaw Mae Bang Hua Diad
blocks.signature: Tak-style Thin Noodles with Dried Shrimp Powder and Pork Crackling, Barbecued Pork in Broth, Sticky Rice on the Grill
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Tak city and want noodles that generations of locals have eaten, Kwaytiaw Mae Bang Hua Diad is the spot. The small shop is on Taksin Road on the Ping riverbank side, just a few hundred metres down the slope from Doi Khiri Temple, and has been running for over 80 years — now in its third generation. The star of the menu is an old-style red pork noodle: pork with just the right marbling, marinated to a family recipe, giving sweet-savoury, faintly sweet red pork served with thin-noodles and topped with dried shrimp powder and pork crackling — a combination that just works.

The most ordered item is the dry tom yam egg noodle — the round noodles are made fresh in-house every day, giving a springy chew you won't get from packet noodles. The broth is made purely from pork bones, lightly seasoned with no MSG, delivering a clean, naturally rounded flavour. Add pork stuffed dumplings to round out the meal; follow it with grilled sticky rice, satay skewers, or the traditional Thai cup cakes sold outside — all available to take home too.

The atmosphere is an old-fashioned local joint, not many tables, busy from late morning. Prices are very approachable at 30–35 THB per bowl — a whole family can eat for well under 100 THB per head. Great for breakfast or a late-morning meal on a budget, or a quick stop on the way north or back to Bangkok.

The shop opens in the morning until early afternoon, roughly 07:30–14:30. Items can sell out before closing. For the headline dishes, come in the late morning. Don't arrive too late in the afternoon. Ratings sit around 3.7 stars on review platforms — a mix of regulars who love the old-school flavour and a few dissenting voices — but the longevity and loyal customer base say something.
blocks.bestFor: Budget breakfast or late-morning noodles; trying Tak's classic old-school bowl
blocks.spice: Your choice — clear broth or tom yam available

blocks.name: Aiyarawadee
blocks.signature: Winged Bean Salad, Bitter Snail Curry, Crispy Pork Leg, Catfish Fried in Fish Sauce
blocks.descHtml:
Ask locals in Tak where to take out-of-town guests for a proper riverside meal and Aiyarawadee is consistently near the top of the list. The restaurant is on the Pa Mamuang side, just across the Ping River bridge, and has been part of the Tak dining scene for years. It suits families, groups of friends, or couples looking for a relaxed evening meal with gentle music and a river breeze.

The dish that reviews mention most is the winged bean salad — many say it lives up to its reputation with a balanced sweet-sour flavour. Next is the bitter snail curry (gaeng khua hoi khom), the restaurant's signature dish. The crispy pork leg — crunchy outside, soft inside — appears on most tables, and the large whole fish — both catfish and sea bass fried in fish sauce with firm flesh and crispy skin — is excellent with hot steamed rice. For something spicy, try the fresh lemongrass salad or the seafood ho mok.

On flavour, most reviews pass comfortably, noting that several dishes tend toward a mellow local sweetness — those who prefer bold, punchy food may want to ask for extra spice. The atmosphere, however, wins universal praise: the restaurant is set at different levels with lush trees, multiple seating spots, and soft amber lantern lighting in the evening that reads as romantic. A small note: the lighting at night is quite dim and some guests find reading the menu difficult.

Per-head cost is approximately 101–250 THB; with large fish or a big group it moves to 250–500 THB. Cash payment gets a 10% discount. Service receives consistent praise for attentiveness. Open roughly 10:00–22:00. Evenings are ideal for catching the river air. Book a riverside table in advance on weekends.
blocks.bestFor: Riverside dinner with family or friends
blocks.libCredit: Illustration: Khao Kha Moo · User:Bi89 / Wikimedia (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Baan Pak Rak Tawan
blocks.area: Mae To Sub-district, Mueang Tak District, Tak Province
blocks.signature: Ribeye Steak, Steamed Tilapia, Grilled Prawns, Fresh Organic Vegetables
blocks.descHtml:
Baan Pak Rak Tawan is a roadside restaurant on Phahon Yothin Road before Tak city — the kind of place drivers regularly pull into — because it is simultaneously a rest stop, a café, and an organic vegetable farm in one. The selling point is produce grown in the on-site plot: fresh, crisp, sweet, chemical-free, harvested and cooked to order. It works well for families who want a healthy, satisfying meal, road-trippers who need a break, or anyone who wants to walk around a pretty vegetable garden and take photos.

Popular orders include large salad bowls — melon salad and crispy vegetable salad made from produce straight from the plot. The signature pork spare-rib steak (the sapha kho curve cut) is a house speciality, alongside steamed tilapia, steamed red tilapia, and miang kham — a Tak province signature where you wrap leaves around a combination of roasted coconut, dried shrimp, lime, chilli, and palm sugar. Reviews mostly praise the fresh vegetables and the well-balanced dressings; the salad portions are large enough to share. Some note that the steak is cooked well and the fried garlic fish is tasty, while a few reviews flag that some dishes can be a little under-seasoned and certain seafood items are frozen. Stick to the vegetable and signature dishes for the best experience.

Prices are accessible — a typical dish runs 50–350 THB; salads 129–219 THB, the pork-rib steak around 339 THB, miang kham 69 THB. Shaded, ample parking, good photo corners in the garden, air-conditioned interior. Open daily 07:00–20:00 — breakfast, lunch, or pick up organic vegetables and local souvenirs to take home.

The restaurant is popular because it ticks all the boxes for the northbound traveller: a good meal, quality produce, and a proper rest break in one stop. Google reviews rate it 4.6 from several thousand ratings. On long weekends it gets busy — book ahead for large groups.
blocks.bestFor: Mid-road-trip stop + a healthy meal with the family

blocks.name: Chailai Dim Sum
blocks.signature: Pork Shumai, Prawn Har Gao, Fried Taro, 50+ dim sum varieties
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Mae Sot and want a full-on breakfast, Chailai Dim Sum is one of the first names locals mention. The restaurant has been open since 2015, right on the Asia Highway next to the lane beside Wat Don Kaew. It's a comfortable air-conditioned room with Chinese-style décor, easy parking out front — welcoming for families who want to eat in peace, road-trippers refuelling before moving on, or large groups since the restaurant seats dozens.

The main draw is a dim sum selection of over 50 varieties, steamed hot and served basket by basket. The items that see the most repeat orders are the pork shumai — firm and well-packed — prawn har gao with springy prawn inside, prawn shumai, crispy-outside-soft-inside fried taro, and steamed buns with cream filling or salted egg lava — several reviews call that one essential. Beyond dim sum there is hot Chinese food: bak kut teh served at a rolling boil with generous toppings, crispy pork that reviewers praise, fried rice, Hokkien-style stir-fried noodles, braised noodles, and various seafood dishes. Easy to lose track of time ordering.

Reviews broadly agree the cooking is solid, ingredients are fresh, and prices are fair — dim sum baskets at 30 THB, single-plate dishes from around 79 THB, most items in the 30–150 THB range. Two to three people eating dim sum won't strain a budget. One thing reviewers note is that individual dim sum pieces are bite-sized, so if you're very hungry you may need several baskets — but at that price it's still good value.

What makes the restaurant popular is the completeness: full dim sum breakfast plus a proper Chinese meal, all in a clean, cool, easy-to-find spot right on the main road. Open daily 08:00–19:00. Come in the morning for the best selection of fresh, hot dim sum. On weekends it gets busy — short queues are normal.
mustOrder: Steamed Bun with Lava / Cream Filling
blocks.bestFor: Dim sum breakfast in Mae Sot — families or groups

blocks.title: Know Before You Eat in Tak

items.title: Getting Around
items.text: Grab is scarce in both Tak city and Mae Sot — don't rely on it. The most practical option is a rental car or motorbike. Several good restaurants are outside the town centres, and Tak city and Mae Sot are roughly 90 minutes apart.

items.title: Payment
items.text: Street stalls, noodle shops, and the clay-pot roti shop operate on cash only. Carry small bills and coins. Some larger sit-down restaurants accept PromptPay, but credit cards are not widely accepted.

items.title: Beating the Queues
items.text: The legendary clay-pot roti opens very early and is typically sold out before 8 a.m. — arrive at dawn. Riverside restaurants and the grilled-prawn shop get crowded on weekends; arrive before noon or before 6 p.m. for a comfortable seat.

items.title: Spice Level
items.text: Local Tak food and the khao soi curry broth can be quite bold. Tell staff "not spicy" or "less spicy" in English and they'll adjust. The Tak-style nam phrik dam and stir-fried spicy dishes are genuinely hot — taste before adding more.

items.title: Language and Menus
items.text: Most local restaurants have Thai-only menus. Some Mae Sot shops have food photos to point at. Google Translate's camera function works well for photographing menus. Staff are friendly and happy to recommend their best dishes.

items.title: Halal and Vegetarian
items.text: Mae Sot has several Muslim restaurants. Tuay Khao Soi is the recommended halal chicken khao soi option. For vegetarians, Baan Pak Rak Tawan near Mae To has a wide organic-vegetable menu with salads and plant-focused dishes.

blocks.title: Making the Most of Both Sides of Tak
blocks.html:
Tak splits its food across two zones about 90 minutes apart. If you only have one day, pick one side. On the Tak city side, start early at Kwaytiaw Mae Bang Hua Diad or another Tak-style noodle shop, then stay for a long lunch or evening at Chidchol or Aiyarawadee on the Ping River. If you're heading north, stop at Thiengna in Mai Ngam for coffee in the middle of the fields.

On the Mae Sot side, chase the clay-pot roti before 8 a.m. because it runs out fast. Head to Tuay Khao Soi or Chailai Dim Sum for lunch, then save the evening for B. Kung Pao Mae Sot and a plate of fat grilled river prawns. Travelling between the two sides, use Baan Pak Rak Tawan near Mae To as a mid-route meal and rest stop.

blocks.text: A great Tak trip needs a well-placed base — whether that's a hotel in Tak city near the Ping River or a spot in Mae Sot close to the market and border crossing. Check availability and latest prices before you go.

faq.q: Which restaurant in Tak is most famous?
faq.a: On the Mae Sot side, the Legendary Clay-Pot Roti — First in Thailand — is the most famous, open for over half a century and baked in an earthen oven. For seafood, B. Kung Pao Mae Sot and its grilled river prawns are the landmark. On the Tak city side, Chidchol on the Ping River is the name locals mention most.

faq.q: What are Tak's signature dishes to try?
faq.a: Tak-style thin noodles topped with dried shrimp powder, pork crackling, and stuffed pork dumplings; grilled river prawns from Mae Sot; halal chicken khao soi at Tuay Khao Soi; clay-pot roti baked in an earthen oven; and miang jom pol — Tak's own leaf-wrap bite — available at Baan Pak Rak Tawan.

Most are wallet-friendly. Tak-style noodles are 30–35 THB per bowl, khao soi 35–60 THB, clay-pot roti 10–30 THB per piece — a full meal under 100 THB. Sit-down spots like Chidchol run 80–400 THB per dish. Grilled river prawns at B. Kung Pao come to around 500–1,000 THB per person.

faq.q: Do I need to book in advance?
faq.a: Street stalls and noodle shops — just walk in. For Ping River dining spots like Chidchol and Aiyarawadee, or B. Kung Pao Mae Sot on a long weekend, call ahead or arrive before peak hours to secure a table.

faq.q: Which restaurants are open for dinner or late?
faq.a: Chidchol, Aiyarawadee, and B. Kung Pao Mae Sot are open for the evening. Tuay Khao Soi has an evening shift. The Legendary Clay-Pot Roti is strictly a breakfast spot — it opens before dawn and sells out long before midday.
